original_value: The relationship between 3D terrain complexity and fine-scale localization and distribution of species is poorly understood. Here we present a very fine-scale 3D reconstruction model of three zones of circalittoral rocky shelf in the Bay of Biscay. Detailed terrain variables are extracted from 3D models using a structure-from-motion (SfM) approach applied to ROTV images. Significant terrain variables that explain species location were selected using general additive models (GAMs) and micro-distribution of the species were predicted. Two models combining BPI, curvature and rugosity can explain 55% and 77% of the Ophiuroidea and Crinoidea distribution, respectively. The third model contributes to explaining the terrain variables that induce the localization of Dendrophyllia cornigera. GAM univariate models detect the terrain variables for each structural species in this third zone (Artemisina transiens, D. cornigera and Phakellia ventilabrum). To avoid the time-consuming task of manual annotation of presence, a deep-learning algorithm (YOLO v4) is proposed. This approach achieves very high reliability and low uncertainty in automatic object detection, identification and location. These new advances applied to underwater imagery (SfM and deep-learning) can resolve the very-high resolution information needed for predictive microhabitat modeling in a very complex zone.

result.paraphrase: The link between 3D terrain complexity and the fine-scale localization and distribution of species remains poorly understood. Here, we present a very high-resolution 3D reconstruction model of three circalittoral rocky shelf zones in the Bay of Biscay. Detailed terrain variables were extracted from 3D models using a structure-from-motion (SfM) method applied to ROTV imagery. General additive models (GAMs) were used to select the significant terrain variables explaining species location and to predict species micro-distribution. Two models combining BPI, curvature, and rugosity explain 55% and 77% of the distribution of Ophiuroidea and Crinoidea, respectively. A third model helps explain the terrain variables driving the localization of Dendrophyllia cornigera. GAM univariate models identify the terrain variables for each structural species in this third zone (Artemisina transiens, D. cornigera, and Phakellia ventilabrum). To avoid the time-consuming manual annotation of presence, a deep-learning algorithm (YOLO v4) is proposed. This approach achieves very high reliability and low uncertainty in automatic object detection, identification, and location. Applied to underwater imagery, these advances in SfM and deep learning can provide the very high-resolution information needed for predictive microhabitat modeling in such a highly complex area.
